overview.intro: This lesson teaches the daily nursing behaviors that keep peripheral IV and urinary catheters safe in dogs and cats: cleaning in before you touch anything, looking closely at the Pet and the system, ensuring the order and your own authorization, accessing aseptically, and responding early when something is wrong. A 2024 UK multicenter veterinary study recorded complications in 102 of 382 peripheral IV catheters, and a prospective teaching-hospital study found positive bacterial cultures in 24 of 116 peripheral catheters — which is why structured, repeated checks are the standard rather than the exception. Urinary catheters create a direct path between the environment and the bladder, and ISCAID names open collection systems, bags above the Pet, and contamination during maintenance as poor-management risks. Written for new hires and experienced team members alike: PetNurses, Nurse Aides, Pet Practitioners, and DVMs.
objectives: Explain how catheter care protects Pet safety, Pet comfort, reliable therapy, infection prevention, team safety, and Hannah documentation standards.
Identify peripheral IV and urinary catheter components, and classify each as touchable after disinfection, a critical part, monitor-only, or an escalation device.
Recognize central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, and hazardous-drug lines as recognition-and-escalation devices outside unsupervised scope.
Apply hand hygiene timing, PPE selection, aseptic non-touch technique, and clean supply handling to every catheter interaction.
Run and document a structured IV site check without diagnosing or assigning unsupported severity grades.
Trace lines before access, verify the order, route, compatibility and your own authorization, and stop at any pump, line, bag, or catheter mismatch.
Maintain urinary drainage as a closed, dependent, unobstructed system, observe output objectively, and sample only from an approved port when authorized.

Respond safely to contamination, disconnection, suspected infiltration or extravasation, obstruction, absent output, sharps and spill risk, and hazardous-drug lines by stopping, protecting, and escalating immediately.
Document objectively, hand off completely, and communicate with Members inside role scope.
overview.connectsForward: Medication Safety taught you to verify before you act. Asepsis and Infection Prevention taught you to protect the Pet from what you cannot see. Catheter Care puts both to work on the devices that stay in a Pet for hours or days. CLEAR LINES carries into fluid therapy, hospitalized patient care, anesthesia support, surgery, and discharge. If you cannot name the line, do not access it. Trace it, verify the order, and ask the DVM or RVT before anything flows.

modules.title: Why Catheter Care Matters
modules.completionHeading: Every line is a safety system
modules.completionBody: You connected catheter care to Pet safety, comfort, reliable therapy, infection prevention, team safety, and documentation. Next: know exactly what you are touching.
modules.content:
Every line into a Pet is a safety system. A peripheral IV catheter carries fluids and medication through the skin barrier; a urinary catheter connects the bladder to the outside world. Catheter care is how Hannah keeps those systems closed, comfortable, reliable, and observed — and how a team member notices trouble early enough to protect the Pet.

Catheter care scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Clean in with hand hygiene and the PPE the task calls for, before touching any line.
  • Look closely at the Pet, site, dressing, tubing, connections, bag, and pump.
  • Trace the line and confirm the order, the route, and your own authorization first.
  • Stop and escalate early — any role, any time, for anything abnormal.

No one does

  • Invent a dwell time, a replacement interval, a catheter size, a flush amount or frequency, or a urinary duration rule.
  • Diagnose phlebitis, thrombosis, or infection, or decide independently that a line must come out.
  • Force a flush, reconnect a contaminated end, or reuse a dropped injection cap.
  • Access a central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, or hazardous-drug line without the required training and authorization.

The order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable instruction in catheter care. This lesson never supplies a dwell time, replacement interval, flush volume or frequency, catheter size, prep recipe, urinary duration, or clinical threshold. AAHA directs that catheter sites be examined and that bandages be replaced when they are not clean and dry (AAHA — IV catheter maintenance), and human CDC guidance appears here only as clearly labelled human-health guidance adapted as a general safety principle (CDC — use of agency materials).

In this module you will

  • Explain how catheter care protects Pet safety, Pet comfort, reliable therapy, infection prevention, team safety, and Hannah documentation standards.
  • Name the five CLEAR LINES steps and what LINES stands for.
  • Recognize that this lesson teaches care, monitoring, authorized access, documentation, and escalation — never placement, diagnosis, or prescribing.

Why this matters

Catheter complications are common enough to expect them

Peripheral IV catheters develop mechanical, inflammatory, and infectious problems often enough that structured, repeated checks are the only reliable defense. A 2024 UK multicenter veterinary study recorded complications in 102 of 382 peripheral IV catheters, with limb swelling and suspected phlebitis, and dislodgement or Pet interference, among the most common categories (Haskey et al.). A prospective veterinary teaching-hospital study found positive bacterial cultures in 24 of 116 peripheral IV catheters, including multidrug-resistant isolates among the positive cultures (Crisi et al.). Neither study gives you a number to apply to a Pet in front of you — they tell you why you look, every time.

Urinary catheters create a direct path between the environment and the bladder. ISCAID identifies poor catheter management, open collection systems, collection bags positioned above the Pet, and contamination during maintenance as factors that let bacteria migrate (ISCAID urinary guidelines). Older veterinary work established indwelling bladder catheters as a route for urinary tract infection in dogs and cats (Barsanti et al.). Closed, low, unkinked, and observed is the whole job.

Catheter care is also team safety. Veterinary standard precautions cover hand hygiene, PPE, sharps handling, spill response, isolation practice, and written infection-control plans with named responsibility and training (NASPHV Compendium, AVMA policy).

Pet comfort

A secure, clean, unkinked line that nobody has to fight with is a calmer hospital stay.

Reliable therapy

Fluids and medication only work if they reach the vein. An occluded or dislodged catheter silently stops therapy.

Infection prevention

Hands, hubs, caps, dressings, and closed systems are the barriers. Every one of them is yours to protect.

Team safety

Sharps, body fluids, hazardous-drug lines, and spills all require the right PPE and the right escalation.

The Hannah framework

CLEAR LINES

CLEAR LINES is a Hannah memory aid for the order of thinking before, during, and after any catheter interaction. It is a teaching device, not a medical protocol and not a substitute for the order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction.

CLEAR LINES step explorer

Guided explorer

Open each letter to see what the step means and the behavior standard behind it. Use the arrow keys to move between letters.

C — Clean in

Hand hygiene, PPE, and protected clean supplies before you touch the catheter, port, dressing, tubing, or collection system. CDC recommends hand hygiene immediately before an aseptic task and immediately after glove removal, and veterinary standard precautions are explicit that gloves do not replace hand hygiene (CDC hand hygiene, NASPHV Compendium).

L — Look closely

Assess the Pet, the site, the dressing, the tubing, the connections, the bag, the pump, and the Pet’s behavior before you use the line. AAHA directs that catheter sites be examined at least twice daily for pain and swelling and that bandages be replaced when not clean and dry (AAHA IV catheter maintenance).

E — Ensure the order

Confirm the Pet, the active order or protocol, the medication or fluid, the route, compatibility, pump settings, line labels, alerts, isolation and hazard status, and your own role authorization before access. AAHA emphasizes that trained nursing staff continually monitor IV fluid administration (AAHA fluid administration and monitoring).

A — Aseptic access

Disinfect the approved hub or port per Hannah protocol and product instructions for use, keep sterile and clean ends protected, and do not touch critical parts after disinfection. CDC recommends scrubbing access ports with an appropriate antiseptic and accessing ports only with sterile devices (CDC intravascular catheter guidance).

R — Respond early

Stop, contain, comfort, and escalate whenever something is abnormal, contaminated, resistant, disconnected, leaking, or outside your authorization. Early escalation is always in scope.

LINES — Leave it closed, intact, noticed, escalated, summarized

Keep IV and urinary systems closed as directed, minimize handling, protect the line from Pet interference, document what you observed and did, and hand off anything unresolved. CDC CAUTI guidance treats a maintained closed drainage system and unobstructed flow as core (CDC CAUTI guidance).

Six things catheter care protects. Select each one, then choose the catheter-care behavior that protects it. Wrong choices explain themselves and stay open so you can try again.

All six protections linked

Catheter care is not one task. It is the same handful of behaviors — clean hands, a close look, a traced line, an aseptic entry, and an early escalation — protecting six different things at once.

What this lesson does not do

This lesson does not teach catheter placement or removal technique, does not diagnose phlebitis, thrombosis, or infection, does not set dwell times or replacement intervals, and does not authorize anyone to access a central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, or hazardous-drug line. Those decisions belong to the order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction.

Catheter care scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Clean in with hand hygiene and the PPE the task calls for, before touching any line.
  • Look closely at the Pet, site, dressing, tubing, connections, bag, and pump.
  • Trace the line and confirm the order, the route, and your own authorization first.
  • Stop and escalate early — any role, any time, for anything abnormal.

No one does

  • Invent a dwell time, a replacement interval, a catheter size, a flush amount or frequency, or a urinary duration rule.
  • Diagnose phlebitis, thrombosis, or infection, or decide independently that a line must come out.
  • Force a flush, reconnect a contaminated end, or reuse a dropped injection cap.
  • Access a central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, or hazardous-drug line without the required training and authorization.

The order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable instruction in catheter care. This lesson never supplies a dwell time, replacement interval, flush volume or frequency, catheter size, prep recipe, urinary duration, or clinical threshold. AAHA directs that catheter sites be examined and that bandages be replaced when they are not clean and dry (AAHA — IV catheter maintenance), and human CDC guidance appears here only as clearly labelled human-health guidance adapted as a general safety principle (CDC — use of agency materials).

In this module you will

  • Name the components of a peripheral IV system and a urinary closed-drainage system.
  • Classify each component as touchable after disinfection, a critical part you do not touch, monitor only, or an escalation device.
  • Recognize central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, and hazardous-drug lines as recognition-and-escalation devices only.
  • Sort care actions into IV, urinary, both, or escalation-only.

Peripheral IV system

From the bag to the vein, every junction is a decision point

A peripheral IV setup may include the catheter in the vein, the catheter hub, an injection cap, a T-port or Y-port, an extension set, the administration set, the pump segment, the dressing, and the securement. AAHA describes attaching a catheter cap, T set, or suitable extension set and securing and covering the catheter with sterile bandage material after placement (AAHA IV catheter maintenance). Every junction is a place where contamination, disconnection, or a wrong-line error can happen.

Urinary closed-drainage system

Closed, low, unkinked, observed

An indwelling urinary system includes the catheter, the securement, the drainage tubing, a sampling port if one is present, and a closed collection bag. AAHA instructs immediate connection to a sterile closed collection system after indwelling urethral catheter placement and anchoring to prevent displacement (AAHA urethral catheter guidance). Human CAUTI guidance, used here as a clearly labelled general safety principle, recommends maintaining the closed system, keeping tubing free of kinks, keeping the bag below the bladder and off the floor, and maintaining unobstructed flow (CDC CAUTI guidance).

Urinary system component reveal

Guided reveal

Open each component to see what you observe, what you protect, and where your role ends.

Indwelling urinary catheter

What do you protect?

Protect it from tension, traction, and Pet interference, and keep the system closed. Placement, duration, and removal decisions belong to the DVM. AAHA directs anchoring to prevent displacement (AAHA urethral catheter guidance).

Securement

What do you check?

Check that the securement is intact and comfortable, with no tension pulling on the catheter and no pressure sore forming. Report anything loose, tight, soiled, or chewed.

Drainage tubing

What do you check?

Check for kinks, loops above the Pet, tension, and tubing trapped under the Pet. Human CAUTI guidance recommends keeping tubing free of kinks and flow unobstructed (CDC CAUTI guidance).

Sampling port

What is your limit?

Sample only from an approved port, only when authorized, and only per protocol. ISCAID states that urine culture should never be performed on urine from the collection bag or any other part of the collection system (ISCAID urinary guidelines).

Collection bag

What do you check?

Bag below the bladder, off the floor, not overfull, spigot protected, and emptied per protocol with a separate clean container while avoiding splash and spigot contact (CDC CAUTI guidance).

Output and urine character

What do you document?

Document what you can observe objectively: presence or absence of urine in the tubing and bag, and the appearance you can see. Absent output with a restless or painful Pet is an immediate escalation, not a wait-and-see. Interpretation belongs to the DVM.

Advanced lines: recognize and escalate

Central venous catheters, PICCs, midlines, arterial lines, intraosseous catheters, and chemotherapy or other hazardous-drug lines are recognition-and-escalation devices in this lesson. CDC guidance states that only trained personnel who demonstrate competence should insert and maintain intravascular catheters (CDC intravascular catheter guidance), and ACVIM consensus restricts handling and administration of cytotoxic drugs to trained personnel (ACVIM cytotoxic consensus). Monitor for leakage, dislodgement, bleeding, pain, and label hazards; escalate immediately; do not access, flush, repair, or dress them unless you are specifically trained and authorized.

Clean in is the step people skip when they are busy, and it is the step that decides whether the next twelve hours of therapy stay safe. Hand hygiene, PPE, protected supplies, an approved port, and an aseptic non-touch entry.

Every team member does

  • Clean in with hand hygiene and the PPE the task calls for, before touching any line.
  • Look closely at the Pet, site, dressing, tubing, connections, bag, and pump.
  • Trace the line and confirm the order, the route, and your own authorization first.
  • Stop and escalate early — any role, any time, for anything abnormal.

  • Invent a dwell time, a replacement interval, a catheter size, a flush amount or frequency, or a urinary duration rule.
  • Diagnose phlebitis, thrombosis, or infection, or decide independently that a line must come out.
  • Force a flush, reconnect a contaminated end, or reuse a dropped injection cap.
  • Access a central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, or hazardous-drug line without the required training and authorization.

The order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable instruction in catheter care. This lesson never supplies a dwell time, replacement interval, flush volume or frequency, catheter size, prep recipe, urinary duration, or clinical threshold. AAHA directs that catheter sites be examined and that bandages be replaced when they are not clean and dry (AAHA — IV catheter maintenance), and human CDC guidance appears here only as clearly labelled human-health guidance adapted as a general safety principle (CDC — use of agency materials).

In this module you will

  • Apply hand hygiene at the right moments for catheter work, including immediately before an aseptic task and immediately after glove removal.
  • Choose PPE based on the exposure the task creates, and change gloves between dirty and clean tasks on the same Pet.
  • Use aseptic non-touch technique: identify critical parts, protect them, and never touch them after disinfection.
  • Respond correctly when a cap, connector, or clean supply becomes contaminated.

Hand hygiene

The moments that matter for catheter work

CDC human healthcare guidance recommends hand hygiene immediately before touching a patient, before an aseptic task, after body-fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient’s surroundings, and immediately after glove removal; this lesson adapts those as general safety principles for veterinary catheter care where veterinary-specific detail is absent (CDC hand hygiene, WHO five moments). CDC intravascular guidance is more specific for lines: perform hand hygiene before and after palpating catheter sites, and before and after accessing or dressing a catheter (CDC intravascular catheter guidance).

Veterinary standard precautions add the rules that matter on a treatment floor: wear gloves when contact with body fluids, urine specimens, contaminated equipment, or a suspected infectious disease is likely, and change gloves between dirty and clean procedures on the same Pet (NASPHV Compendium). Gloves are a barrier, not a substitute for clean hands.

BeforeHand hygiene, then gather and protect your supplies. Keep clean ends clean.
Before touchHand hygiene again immediately before the aseptic task — the last thing before you enter the system.
DuringAseptic non-touch technique: only approved, disinfected surfaces; never a critical part.
AfterRemove PPE, hand hygiene immediately after glove removal, then document.

Aseptic access sequence

Sequence practice

Put the eleven steps of an authorized catheter access in order. Choosing a step too early explains why and does not place it.

Steps — choose them in order
Your sequence so far
    Access sequence complete

    Verify, gather, clean hands, PPE, protect, identify, trace, disinfect, enter without touching, close, and document. The order is what keeps it aseptic.

    Aseptic non-touch technique

    Name the critical part, then protect it

    Aseptic non-touch technique is simple to state and easy to lose: identify the parts of the system that must stay clean or sterile, protect them for the whole task, and never touch them after disinfection. CDC recommends minimizing contamination risk by scrubbing access ports with an appropriate antiseptic and accessing ports only with sterile devices; the agent, the contact and dry time, the device, and the technique come from the order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction (CDC intravascular catheter guidance).

    Critical parts

    Port and cap entry surfaces, syringe tips, needle-free connector faces, the inside of a sterile cap, and the catheter hub after disinfection.

    Contaminated the moment they touch anything

    A dropped cap, a syringe tip laid on a table, a connector touched with a bare finger, a supply opened and left waiting.

    Protected

    Ends kept capped or covered, supplies opened at the point of use, and disinfected surfaces entered with a sterile device.

    Contaminated hub decisions

    Decision practice

    Four moments where something becomes contaminated. Choose the safe action; the panel then explains why each alternative is not appropriate.

    • Contamination · dropped cap

      A dog’s IV line was disconnected for an approved walk. The injection cap falls on the floor before you reconnect. What do you do?

    • Contamination · touched port

      You disinfect the port, then steady it with a bare fingertip before connecting the syringe. What now?

    • Supplies · opened early

      At the start of the shift a colleague opened flush syringes and caps and left them on a tray for later. What is the right response?

    • PPE · dirty to clean

      You have just emptied a urinary collection bag with gloves on. The same Pet needs an authorized IV port access next. What do you do?

    Practice complete

    Scenario 2 — the dropped cap

    A dog’s IV line is disconnected for a brief approved walk. The cap falls on the floor before reconnection. The safe answer is in the decision set above: do not reuse it, protect the exposed connection, obtain an approved replacement, disinfect and cap per protocol and authorization, and notify if contamination may have occurred. AAHA states that disconnected IV connection sites should be cleaned with isopropyl alcohol and capped with injection caps, that single-use wipes should be used, and that injection caps should not be reused (AAHA IV catheter maintenance).

Looking closely is a skill with a structure. You are not deciding what is wrong — you are describing what you see, deciding whether the line is safe to use, and escalating early. Describe, decide, escalate, document.

Catheter care scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Clean in with hand hygiene and the PPE the task calls for, before touching any line.
  • Look closely at the Pet, site, dressing, tubing, connections, bag, and pump.
  • Trace the line and confirm the order, the route, and your own authorization first.
  • Stop and escalate early — any role, any time, for anything abnormal.

No one does

  • Invent a dwell time, a replacement interval, a catheter size, a flush amount or frequency, or a urinary duration rule.
  • Diagnose phlebitis, thrombosis, or infection, or decide independently that a line must come out.
  • Force a flush, reconnect a contaminated end, or reuse a dropped injection cap.
  • Access a central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, or hazardous-drug line without the required training and authorization.

The order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable instruction in catheter care. This lesson never supplies a dwell time, replacement interval, flush volume or frequency, catheter size, prep recipe, urinary duration, or clinical threshold. AAHA directs that catheter sites be examined and that bandages be replaced when they are not clean and dry (AAHA — IV catheter maintenance), and human CDC guidance appears here only as clearly labelled human-health guidance adapted as a general safety principle (CDC — use of agency materials).

In this module you will

  • Run a structured IV site check: site, dressing, securement, limb and paw, tubing, connections, and Pet behavior.
  • Describe findings objectively without assigning a diagnosis or an unsupported severity grade.
  • Decide between continue monitoring, stop use, protect and escalate, and act-within-role.
  • Respond correctly to suspected infiltration or extravasation during an authorized administration.

What to look for

The findings veterinary research actually describes

AAHA recommends examining the catheter site at least twice daily, evaluating for pain, swelling, and thrombophlebitis, and replacing the bandage if it is not clean and dry (AAHA IV catheter maintenance). The 2024 UK veterinary study categorized peripheral IV catheter complications as discharge from the site, dislodgement or Pet interference, limb swelling or suspected phlebitis, occlusion, and soiled bandaging, and defined occlusion as increased resistance or an inability to flush or administer medication, and soiled bandaging as moisture or contamination requiring replacement (Haskey et al.).

Notice what those categories are: descriptions. “Limb swelling” and “suspected phlebitis” are observations plus a concern, not a diagnosis. This lesson teaches no grading scale and no severity threshold. You describe, you follow Hannah stop-use and escalation rules, and the DVM interprets.

Continue monitoring

Dressing clean, dry, intact and appropriately snug; site comfortable; limb and paw match the opposite side; Pet relaxed; line traced and patent per the order. Document the normal check.

Act within role

A correctable, low-risk finding such as tubing caught under the Pet or a bag out of position. Correct it if it is within your role, then document and mention it at handoff.

Stop use and escalate

Pain, swelling, redness, warmth or coolness, leakage, discharge, odor, damp or soiled dressing, resistance to flush, or a paw that has changed. Stop, keep the Pet calm, protect the line, notify.

Escalate immediately

Bleeding, a broken or disconnected line, suspected infiltration or extravasation, a hazardous-drug concern, an advanced line, or a Pet in distress.

Dressing integrity

Four layers, four questions

A dressing has a job: protect the insertion site, secure the catheter and line, stay clean and dry, and let you see and feel the limb around it. When any of those fail, the dressing is a finding, not just a bandage.

Contact layer at the site Is it clean, dry, and undisturbed? Any strike-through moisture, discharge, or odor is a finding.
Securement Is the catheter held without traction or a pressure point? Is any tape chewed, loose, or slipped?
Outer wrap Is it snug without constricting? Can you assess the limb and paw above and below it?
The limb and paw around it Are they the same size, temperature, and comfort as the opposite side? A change here outranks a tidy-looking bandage.

  • Dressing 2 · damp edge

  • Dressing 3 · tight wrap, puffy paw

    The wrap looks neat but tight, and the paw below it is puffy and cooler than the opposite paw.

  • Dressing 4 · chewed tape, line under tension

    The tape is chewed through on one side and the extension set is under visible tension where the dog has moved.

modules.content:
Trace before touch; verify before flow. Wrong-line, wrong-route, wrong-Pet, and pump errors are prevented in the ten seconds before you connect anything — and almost never afterward.

Catheter care scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Clean in with hand hygiene and the PPE the task calls for, before touching any line.
  • Look closely at the Pet, site, dressing, tubing, connections, bag, and pump.
  • Trace the line and confirm the order, the route, and your own authorization first.
  • Stop and escalate early — any role, any time, for anything abnormal.

No one does

  • Invent a dwell time, a replacement interval, a catheter size, a flush amount or frequency, or a urinary duration rule.
  • Diagnose phlebitis, thrombosis, or infection, or decide independently that a line must come out.
  • Force a flush, reconnect a contaminated end, or reuse a dropped injection cap.
  • Access a central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, or hazardous-drug line without the required training and authorization.

The order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable instruction in catheter care. This lesson never supplies a dwell time, replacement interval, flush volume or frequency, catheter size, prep recipe, urinary duration, or clinical threshold. AAHA directs that catheter sites be examined and that bandages be replaced when they are not clean and dry (AAHA — IV catheter maintenance), and human CDC guidance appears here only as clearly labelled human-health guidance adapted as a general safety principle (CDC — use of agency materials).

In this module you will

  • Trace a line from its source through the pump and tubing to the Pet before access or administration.
  • Verify the Pet, the order, the route, compatibility, the pump settings, the line label, and your own authorization.
  • Recognize pump, line, bag, and catheter mismatches that require stopping and escalating.
  • Apply Hannah and AAHA line and bag safety habits without inventing flush volumes or schedules.

Line and bag safety

What AAHA actually says

AAHA fluid therapy guidance states that a new IV line and bag should be used for each patient, that IV lines should be primed before use to avoid air embolism, and that IV fluid bags should not be used for saline flushes because of contamination risk (AAHA fluid administration and monitoring). The same guidance states that trained nursing staff should continually monitor IV fluid administration and that inadequate monitoring can compromise patient care.

AAHA’s 2024 fluid guidelines also warn that one fluid rate does not fit all and that fluid overload is potentially life-threatening and most commonly caused by excessive fluid administration (AAHA 2024 fluid therapy guidelines). That is exactly why the rate on the pump is checked against the order for this Pet, every time, by the person about to start it.

Flushing happens only per the order, Hannah protocol, and the product instructions for use. A 2024 veterinary observational study discusses flushing practice patterns, but a study’s observed practice is not a Hannah instruction: this lesson does not give you a volume, a solution, or a frequency (Haskey et al.).

Line-tracing simulation

Tracing simulation

Trace the path in order, from the source to the Pet. Selecting a segment out of order explains why and does not place it.

    Source, pump, set, junctions, near-catheter components, catheter, Pet, then access or stop. Eight steps, about ten seconds, and it is the difference between a safe dose and a wrong-line event.

    Order and compatibility check

    Verification builder

      Pet, order, authorization, line, mismatch response, aseptic access and documentation. Notice that two of the six steps are about you and the line rather than the drug — that is where wrong-line events are caught.

      Scenario 4 — pump running, line not traced

      A pump is infusing into one of two lines near a Pet. One line leads to a peripheral IV catheter and the other is part of a urinary collection system. The correct response is to trace from the bag through the pump and tubing to the Pet before touching or administering anything, and to stop and escalate if the line or the route is unclear. Do not silence the pump and assume the labelled bag is correct, do not disconnect and reconnect both systems, and do not ask the Member which line was used earlier (AAHA fluid administration and monitoring).

        The pump shows it is infusing, but you find the line clamped below the pump.

      • Mismatch 3 · wrong catheter type

        The only accessible line on this Pet is a urinary catheter, but the order is for an IV medication.

      • Mismatch 4 · hazardous-drug label

modules.completionBody: You can audit a drainage setup, correct what is yours to correct, and escalate absent output without manipulating the system. Next: responding, documenting, and handing off.
modules.content:
Closed, low, unkinked, observed, escalated. A urinary catheter is the shortest path from the outside world to the bladder, and almost everything that protects it is positioning, restraint from unnecessary handling, and noticing early.

Catheter care scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Clean in with hand hygiene and the PPE the task calls for, before touching any line.
  • Look closely at the Pet, site, dressing, tubing, connections, bag, and pump.
  • Trace the line and confirm the order, the route, and your own authorization first.
  • Stop and escalate early — any role, any time, for anything abnormal.

No one does

  • Invent a dwell time, a replacement interval, a catheter size, a flush amount or frequency, or a urinary duration rule.
  • Diagnose phlebitis, thrombosis, or infection, or decide independently that a line must come out.
  • Force a flush, reconnect a contaminated end, or reuse a dropped injection cap.
  • Access a central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, or hazardous-drug line without the required training and authorization.

The order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable instruction in catheter care. This lesson never supplies a dwell time, replacement interval, flush volume or frequency, catheter size, prep recipe, urinary duration, or clinical threshold. AAHA directs that catheter sites be examined and that bandages be replaced when they are not clean and dry (AAHA — IV catheter maintenance), and human CDC guidance appears here only as clearly labelled human-health guidance adapted as a general safety principle (CDC — use of agency materials).

In this module you will

  • Maintain a closed, dependent, unobstructed urinary drainage system within your role.
  • Audit a drainage setup and find every positioning, tension, kink, and contamination issue.
  • Observe output and urine character objectively and escalate absent output, obstruction concern, leakage, contamination, pain, or distress immediately.
  • Sample only from an approved port, per protocol, when authorized — and never from the collection bag.

The closed system

Why closed matters more than clean-looking

AAHA directs immediate connection to a sterile closed collection system after indwelling urethral catheter placement, and anchoring the catheter to prevent displacement (AAHA urethral catheter guidance). Human CAUTI guidance, used here as clearly labelled human-health guidance adapted as a general safety principle, recommends maintaining a closed drainage system, replacing the catheter and collecting system using aseptic technique if breaks in aseptic technique, disconnection, or leakage occur, keeping catheter and tubing free of kinks, keeping the collection bag below the bladder and off the floor, and emptying regularly with a separate clean container while avoiding splash and spigot contact (CDC CAUTI guidance). Hannah protocol and DVM direction govern what any given team member actually does.

ISCAID adds two rules that come up constantly on a treatment floor: urine culture should never be performed on urine from the collection bag or any other part of the collection system, and prophylactic antimicrobials to prevent cystitis in catheterized animals are not indicated, with routine catheter replacement solely to prevent bacteriuria or cystitis also not recommended (ISCAID urinary guidelines). Duration and removal are clinical decisions based on the Pet’s need, reassessed by the DVM.

Tubing, kinks, and bag position decisions

Required scenario 3

Four positioning moments. Choose the safe response.

    A dog with an indwelling urinary catheter is resting in a run. The collection bag is below the Pet but resting on the floor, and the tubing is kinked under the Pet.

  • Positioning · transport

    The bag is nearly full and protocol authorizes you to empty it.

  • Positioning · the Pet is lying on the tubing

Absent output: a decision tree

Required scenario 6

A hospitalized cat has no visible urine in the tubing since the last check and is restless. Work through it one step at a time.

Decision 1 — first move

A hospitalized cat with an indwelling urinary catheter has no visible urine in the tubing since the last check. The cat is restless. The tubing is not obviously kinked. What do you do first?

Decision 2 — the order and the context

The cat is tense and guarding the abdomen. What context do you confirm?

Decision 3 — the system

What do you inspect, within your role, before escalating?

Decision 4 — manipulation

Positioning is correct and there is still no output. A colleague suggests you flush it.

Decision 5 — escalation and record

You are escalating. What do you say and write?

Actions you have taken
    Case handled correctly

    Pet first, context second, the whole path third, no manipulation, immediate escalation, objective record. Nothing in that sequence required you to decide why the output stopped.

    What absent output is not

    Absent output is not a reason to flush a urinary catheter, raise the bag to create back-pressure, disconnect the tubing to “help it drain,” or wait for the next scheduled round. Human CAUTI guidance calls for maintaining unobstructed flow and a closed system, and ISCAID emphasizes reassessing catheter need rather than manipulating the system on a schedule (CDC CAUTI guidance, ISCAID urinary guidelines). Absent output with a restless or painful Pet is an immediate escalation.

    The two that do not belong are both clinical decisions: catheter duration and antimicrobial use. Everything else is daily nursing behavior.

Respond, document, hand off, and talk to the Member inside your role. This is where an observation becomes a protected Pet, a clear record, and a Member who trusts what Hannah told them.

Catheter care scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Clean in with hand hygiene and the PPE the task calls for, before touching any line.
  • Look closely at the Pet, site, dressing, tubing, connections, bag, and pump.
  • Trace the line and confirm the order, the route, and your own authorization first.
  • Stop and escalate early — any role, any time, for anything abnormal.

No one does

  • Invent a dwell time, a replacement interval, a catheter size, a flush amount or frequency, or a urinary duration rule.
  • Diagnose phlebitis, thrombosis, or infection, or decide independently that a line must come out.
  • Force a flush, reconnect a contaminated end, or reuse a dropped injection cap.
  • Access a central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, or hazardous-drug line without the required training and authorization.

The order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable instruction in catheter care. This lesson never supplies a dwell time, replacement interval, flush volume or frequency, catheter size, prep recipe, urinary duration, or clinical threshold. In this module you will

  • Respond safely to a disconnected or leaking line, a contamination event, a sharps risk, and a spill.
  • Recognize a hazardous-drug line and escalate instead of handling it.
  • Build an objective catheter-care note with time, findings, action, and notification.
  • Write a clinical handoff and a Member-safe message that stays inside role scope.

Respond early

Contamination, disconnection, sharps, and spills

AAHA states that disconnected IV connection sites should be cleaned with isopropyl alcohol, capped with injection caps, that single-use wipes should be used, and that injection caps should not be reused (AAHA IV catheter maintenance). Veterinary standard precautions direct immediate containment of potentially infective spills with absorbent material, PPE appropriate to the substance and disinfectant, leak-proof disposal, cleaning and disinfection, and keeping people and animals away until disinfection is complete (NASPHV Compendium).

The same standard precautions are specific about sharps: containers must be puncture- and leak-proof and must not be overfilled, needles must not be bent or passed uncapped, caps must not be held in the mouth, and uncapped needles must not be removed from syringes by hand (NASPHV Compendium). OSHA has interpreted the bloodborne pathogens standard as applying to veterinary clinics where employees have occupational exposure to human blood or other potentially infectious materials (OSHA veterinary interpretation, OSHA 1910.1030).

Hazardous-drug lines end the task for anyone not trained and authorized. NIOSH recommends a protective program for veterinary healthcare workers exposed to hazardous drugs, and ACVIM consensus states that only trained personnel should handle and administer chemotherapeutics (NIOSH hazardous drugs, ACVIM cytotoxic consensus).

Disconnection or exposed end

Stop use. Protect both ends. Do not reconnect contaminated ends. Clean, cap, or replace only per protocol and authorization. Notify and document.

Contaminated cap or critical part

Do not reuse. Obtain an approved replacement. Notify if contamination of the system may have occurred.

Sharps and waste

Puncture- and leak-proof container, never overfilled, no hand recapping, no bending, no uncapped transport.

Spill, leak, or hazardous drug

Contain, PPE, restrict the area, follow the spill protocol, and notify trained authorized personnel immediately.

Disconnected line response

    A catheter-care note answers five questions: what did you observe, when, what did you do, whom did you notify, and what happens next. It does not answer “what is wrong with this Pet” — that is the DVM’s answer to give.

modules.title: CLEAR LINES Job Aid and Knowledge Check
modules.content:
One page to keep where you work, a seven-case recap, a competency self-check, and the graded knowledge check. Ten questions, eighty percent to pass, and remediation named by domain if a critical area is missed.

Catheter care scope — every module

Every team member does

  • Clean in with hand hygiene and the PPE the task calls for, before touching any line.
  • Look closely at the Pet, site, dressing, tubing, connections, bag, and pump.
  • Trace the line and confirm the order, the route, and your own authorization first.
  • Stop and escalate early — any role, any time, for anything abnormal.

No one does

  • Invent a dwell time, a replacement interval, a catheter size, a flush amount or frequency, or a urinary duration rule.
  • Diagnose phlebitis, thrombosis, or infection, or decide independently that a line must come out.
  • Force a flush, reconnect a contaminated end, or reuse a dropped injection cap.
  • Access a central, PICC, midline, arterial, intraosseous, or hazardous-drug line without the required training and authorization.

The order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction govern every variable instruction in catheter care. This lesson never supplies a dwell time, replacement interval, flush volume or frequency, catheter size, prep recipe, urinary duration, or clinical threshold. AAHA directs that catheter sites be examined and that bandages be replaced when they are not clean and dry (AAHA — IV catheter maintenance), and human CDC guidance appears here only as clearly labelled human-health guidance adapted as a general safety principle (CDC — use of agency materials).

In this module you will

  • Recall the CLEAR LINES steps without prompting and apply them to a mini-case.
  • Use the printable one-page job aid at the cage side.
  • Pass the ten-question knowledge check at 80 percent, with remediation for any critical domain missed.

CLEAR LINES recap cases

Two-stage recap

Seven mini-cases, one per module. For each one, choose the CLEAR LINES step first, then choose the action.

Module 1 — A Nurse Aide asks why the IV site has to be checked again when it looked fine two hours ago.

Step 1 — which CLEAR LINES step is this?

Step 2 — what is the action?

Look closely, every time, and teach the habit to the next team member.

Module 2 — You find a line labelled “midline” on a hospitalized dog and you are asked to give an IV medication through it.

Step 1 — which CLEAR LINES step is this?

Step 2 — what is the action?

If you cannot name it and you are not authorized for it, it is an escalation device.

Module 3 — You disinfect the port, then steady it with a bare fingertip before connecting.

Step 1 — which CLEAR LINES step is this?

Step 2 — what is the action?

Name the critical part, protect it, and never touch it after disinfection.

Module 4 — A cat’s paw below the dressing is puffy and cooler than the other paw.

Step 1 — which CLEAR LINES step is this?

Step 2 — what is the action?

Respond early. You do not need to know why to know it is not safe to use.

Module 5 — A pump is running into one of two lines and you cannot tell which one.

Step 1 — which CLEAR LINES step is this?

Step 2 — what is the action?

Trace before touch; verify before flow.

Module 6 — A dog’s urinary collection bag is resting on the run floor with the tubing kinked underneath the Pet.

Step 1 — which CLEAR LINES step is this?

Step 2 — what is the action?

Leave it closed. Correct what is yours to correct and escalate the rest.

Module 7 — A Member asks what the swelling near their Pet’s catheter means.

Step 1 — which CLEAR LINES step is this?

Step 2 — what is the action?

Summarize to the Member inside your scope, and route the medical meaning to the DVM.

All seven cases cleared

Clean in, look closely, ensure the order, aseptic access, respond early, and leave it closed, intact, noticed, escalated, and summarized. If you cannot name the line, do not access it. Trace it, verify the order, and ask the DVM or RVT before anything flows.

Progressive recap

Progressive recap

Ten points, revealed one at a time. Use it as a self-quiz: predict the next point before you reveal it.

  • Every line is a safety system

    A peripheral IV catheter crosses the skin barrier and a urinary catheter connects the bladder to the environment. Catheter care keeps both closed, comfortable, reliable, and observed.

  • Name it before you touch it

    Peripheral IV, urinary, or an advanced device you are not authorized to access. Touchable after disinfection, critical part, monitor only, or escalation device.

  • Clean in is four things

    Hand hygiene at the right moment, task-appropriate PPE, protected supplies, and an approved disinfected port entered without touching critical parts.

  • Gloves are not hand hygiene

    Change gloves between dirty and clean tasks on the same Pet, and perform hand hygiene immediately after glove removal.

  • Describe, do not diagnose

    Pain, swelling, redness, warmth or coolness, leakage, discharge, odor, dressing status, securement, limb and paw comparison, and Pet behavior. No grades, no conclusions.

  • Trace before touch; verify before flow

    Source, pump, set, junctions, near-catheter components, catheter, Pet. Then the order, the route, the compatibility, and your own authorization.

  • Do not force anything

    Resistance on a flush, absent urine output, and unexplained swelling are all escalations. Forcing converts a concern into an injury.

  • Closed, low, unkinked, observed

    Urinary systems stay closed and dependent, tubing stays free of kinks and tension, the bag stays below the Pet and off the floor, and the bag is never a sampling source.

  • Contamination is replaced, not rescued

    A dropped cap, a touched port, or a pre-opened supply is replaced. Protect exposed ends and never reconnect contaminated ones.

  • Write it plainly and hand it off

    Time, findings, action, notification, and plan. Then tell the Member what the team observed and did, and let the DVM carry the medical meaning. If you cannot name the line, do not access it. Trace it, verify the order, and ask the DVM or RVT before anything flows.

Recap complete

Ten points, five letters, one habit. Keep the job aid where the lines are.

Hannah Standards in Practice

Ten proposed standards for catheter care

These are proposed Hannah standards drawn from this lesson’s sources, pending clinical review. They describe behavior, not clinical thresholds.

Clean hands, then the hubHand hygiene immediately before every aseptic catheter task and immediately after glove removal.
Trace before touchEvery access begins with a traced line from the source to the Pet.
Verify before flowPet, order, route, compatibility, pump, line label, and role authorization, every time.
Approved port onlyDisinfect and enter only the approved port, per protocol and product IFU, without touching critical parts.
Never reuse a dropped capA contaminated critical part is replaced, never wiped or rinsed back into service.
Compare, do not gradeDescribe findings and compare with the opposite side; grading and diagnosis belong to the DVM.
Do not force itResistance, absent output, and unexplained swelling are escalations, not obstacles.
Closed, low, unkinkedUrinary systems stay closed and dependent, tubing stays free, and the bag stays below the Pet and off the floor.
Hazard means stopA hazardous-drug label or an advanced line ends the task for anyone not trained and authorized.
Write it plainlyObjective, timed, action-focused notes with the notification recorded, and nothing unresolved left unhanded-off.

Printable job aid

CLEAR LINES catheter care, one page

Print this and keep it where lines are accessed. It prints on its own, without the rest of the app.

CLEAR LINES Catheter Care Job Aid

C — Clean in

Hand hygiene before catheter contact, before an aseptic task, after body-fluid exposure, after touching contaminated surfaces, and immediately after gloves come off. PPE for body-fluid, urine, contaminated-equipment, suspected-infectious, hazardous-drug, or spill risk. Gloves never replace hand hygiene.

L — Look closely (IV)

Pain, swelling, redness, warmth or coolness, leakage, discharge, odor, dressing clean or dry or intact, securement, limb and paw compared with the opposite side, and Pet behavior.

L — Look closely (urinary)

Closed system, dependent drainage, tubing kinks or tension, bag below the Pet and off the floor, securement, output and urine observations, leakage, contamination, and Pet comfort.

E — Ensure the order

Before access, administration, flushing, or sampling: Pet, order, route, line, compatibility, medication or fluid, pump settings, catheter type, role authorization, hazard and isolation status, protocol, and product IFU.

A — Aseptic access

Disinfect only the approved hub or port per Hannah protocol and product IFU. Keep sterile and clean ends protected. Never reuse a dropped cap. Never touch a critical part after disinfection.

R — Respond early

Stop and escalate for contamination, disconnection, line break, resistance or occlusion, swelling, pain, leakage, bleeding, suspected infiltration or extravasation, infection signs, absent urine output, obstruction, hazardous-drug concern, spill or leak, or Pet distress.

LINES — Leave it closed, intact, noticed, escalated, summarized

Keep systems closed, avoid unnecessary manipulation, protect from Pet interference, document objective findings, and hand off anything unresolved.

Never from this job aid

A dwell time, a replacement interval, a catheter size, a flush volume or frequency, a prep recipe, a urinary duration, or a clinical threshold. Those come from the order, the product IFU, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction.

If you cannot name the line, do not access it. Trace it, verify the order, and ask the DVM or RVT before anything flows.

Competency self-check

Self-assessment

Eleven behaviors. Check the ones you could do unsupervised today, within your role. This is a self-assessment and is not scored or stored.

Sources, media rights, and clinical review

Every clinical statement in this lesson is anchored to the sources listed below. No third-party media is bundled or embedded: the four Hannah video placeholders are original productions, and external material with unclear, commercial, or platform-controlled licensing — including veterinary journal photo sequences and public video platforms — is referenced by link only. A CC BY-SA human closed-drainage diagram (Wikimedia Commons) was reviewed as inspiration only and deliberately not adapted, so no share-alike obligation attaches to Hannah material (Commons reuse guidance). CDC material is public domain with attribution and no endorsement implied (CDC use of agency materials); WHO publications carry their own licensing that requires permission for some figures (WHO copyright). All clinical content requires Hannah clinical review before production use. Nothing here replaces the order, the product instructions for use, Hannah protocol, the Pet’s status, and DVM or RVT direction.

quiz.q: Q1 · CLEAR LINES — Clean in · Multiple choiceWhich action best matches CLEAR LINES — Clean in before catheter access?
opts: Touch the port first to check whether it is dry.
Open all supplies at the start of the shift so access is faster later.
Perform hand hygiene, choose the PPE the task needs, protect clean supplies, and access only the approved, disinfected port.
Skip hand hygiene if gloves will be worn.
quiz.exp: Clean in is hand hygiene, PPE selection, protected supplies, and an approved disinfected port — every time, in that order.

quiz.q: Q2 · IV site findings · Select all that applyWhich set contains only findings that should be documented and escalated rather than treated as routine? Choose the complete correct set.
opts: New pain or guarding; paw or limb swelling; leakage or discharge; odor or a damp, soiled dressing.
New pain or guarding; paw or limb swelling; a clean, dry, intact dressing with a comfortable Pet.
A clean, dry, intact dressing; a Pet resting quietly; a bag hanging below the Pet.
Odor or damp dressing; leakage or discharge; the Pet sleeping through the check.
quiz.exp: Pain or guarding, limb or paw swelling, leakage or discharge, and odor or a damp, soiled dressing are all document-and-escalate findings. A clean, dry, intact dressing is documented as the baseline, not escalated.

quiz.q: Q3 · Urinary bag position · Multiple choiceA urinary collection bag is hanging above the Pet. What is the safest response?
opts: Leave it, because gravity does not affect a closed system.
Disconnect the tubing and drain it into a container.
Collect a urine culture from the bag while you are there.
Move the bag below bladder level and off the floor if that is within your role, keep the system closed, and notify if flow or contamination concerns remain.
quiz.exp: Correct the position within your role, keep the system closed, and escalate remaining concerns. Never raise the bag, never disconnect for convenience, and never culture from the bag.

quiz.q: Q4 · Flush volumes and schedules · True or falseThis lesson authorizes team members to choose universal flush volumes and schedules for all peripheral IV catheters.
opts: True
False
quiz.exp: False. This lesson never supplies a flush volume or frequency; those come from the order, protocol, product IFU, and DVM or RVT direction.

quiz.q: Q5 · Dropped injection cap · Multiple choiceAn injection cap falls on the floor before an IV line is reconnected. What is correct?
opts: Do not reuse it. Protect the connection and obtain an approved replacement per protocol and authorization.
Reuse it after wiping it with dry gauze.
Reuse it after rinsing it with sterile saline.
Put it in the Pet’s kennel so it is handy for later.
quiz.exp: A dropped cap is contaminated and is never reused. Protect the connection and get an approved replacement per protocol.

quiz.q: Q6 · Observation to first action · MatchingMatch each observation to its best first action. 1 — pump running with an unclear line path; 2 — urinary tubing kinked under the Pet; 3 — chemotherapy label on an IV setup; 4 — clean, dry IV dressing with a comfortable Pet.
opts: 1 → monitor and document; 2 → trace and verify; 3 → keep the system closed; 4 → escalate to trained personnel.
1 → trace and verify before any access, stopping if unclear; 2 → escalate to hazardous-drug-trained personnel; 3 → monitor and document; 4 → keep the system closed.
1 → keep the system closed; 2 → monitor and document; 3 → trace and verify; 4 → escalate to trained personnel.

1 → trace and verify before any access, stopping if unclear; 2 → keep the system closed and correct safe positioning within role; 3 → do not handle unless trained and authorized, escalate; 4 → monitor and document per protocol.
quiz.exp: 1-A, 2-B, 3-D, 4-C: trace the unclear path, correct the kink within role while keeping the system closed, escalate the hazardous-drug label to trained personnel, and monitor and document the normal dressing.

quiz.q: Q7 · Member communication · Multiple choiceWhich statement is most appropriate for a Member when a catheter-site concern is noticed?
opts: “This always happens after 24 hours.”
“The team noticed swelling near Bella’s catheter site, stopped using that line, and the DVM is evaluating next steps.”
“The catheter caused phlebitis, so the treatment failed.”
“The DVM will probably prescribe antibiotics.”
quiz.exp: Describe what the team observed and did, and point to the DVM for medical meaning. Never diagnose, never predict treatment, and never invent a timeline.

quiz.q: Q8 · Urinary care principles · Select all that applyWhich set contains only urinary catheter care principles taught in this lesson? Choose the complete correct set.
opts: Closed dependent drainage; avoid unnecessary manipulation; keep tubing free of kinks; decide catheterization duration from this lesson.
Closed dependent drainage; keep tubing free of kinks; give prophylactic antimicrobials to prevent cystitis; sample from the approved port.
Closed dependent drainage; avoid unnecessary manipulation; keep tubing free of kinks; sample only from the approved port per protocol when authorized.
Keep the bag above the Pet so it stays clean; avoid unnecessary manipulation; keep tubing free of kinks; sample from the approved port.
quiz.exp: Closed dependent drainage, minimal manipulation, kink-free tubing, and approved-port sampling when authorized. Duration and antimicrobial decisions are clinical, not nursing, decisions.

quiz.q: Q9 · Documentation · Multiple choiceWhich documentation entry is best?
opts: “Catheter looks bad.”

“IV catheter left cephalic: dressing damp at distal edge; paw mildly swollen compared with opposite paw; Pet pulled limb away on touch; fluids stopped; RVT Jamie notified at 14:10; awaiting assessment.”
“Pet is infected.”
“Probably thrombosis; removed because I thought it was time.”
quiz.exp: The best entry describes what was observed, compares it with the other side, states what was done, and names who was notified and when — without diagnosing.

quiz.q: Q10 · Using human guidance · True or falseHuman CDC guidance may be used in this lesson only when it is clearly identified as human-health guidance adapted as a general safety principle, and only when it does not override veterinary sources, Hannah protocol, product instructions for use, the Pet’s status, or DVM or RVT direction.
opts: True
False
quiz.exp: True. Human-health guidance is used only as clearly labelled, adapted general safety principle, and it never overrides veterinary guidance, Hannah protocol, product IFU, the Pet’s status, or DVM or RVT direction.
